content: The time required to complete the procedure using the intervention (medication with mifepristone) was longer compared to the time required with the comparison group (mechanical methods). The certainty of evidence supporting this finding is low. Women in the intervention group (medication) reported lower satisfaction rates compared to women in the comparison group (mechanical methods). The certainty of evidence for this outcome is moderate. Healthcare providers expressed lower satisfaction with the intervention (medication) compared to the comparison (mechanical methods). The certainty of evidence for this finding is high. A higher proportion of women in the intervention group (medication) experienced side effects such as vomiting or diarrhea compared to the comparison group (mechanical methods). The certainty of evidence for this outcome is low. More women in the intervention group (medication) experienced the complication of pre-procedure expulsion compared to the comparison group (mechanical methods). The certainty of evidence for this finding is low. Women in the intervention group (medication) reported higher pain scores compared to women in the comparison group (mechanical methods). The certainty of evidence for this outcome is low. The balance of effects generally favors the comparison group over the intervention group. For Sub-PICO 3, which compared medical methods combined with laminaria versus laminaria alone, the following findings were observed: Pre-procedure cervical dilation was greater in the intervention group (medication + laminaria) compared to the comparison group (laminaria alone). The certainty of evidence is high. Fewer women in the intervention group (medication + laminaria) required further dilation compared to the comparison group (laminaria alone). The certainty of evidence is high. The ease of the procedure was greater in the intervention group (medication + laminaria) compared to the comparison group (laminaria alone). The certainty of evidence is high. The time to complete the procedure was shorter in the intervention group (medication + laminaria) compared to the comparison group (laminaria alone). The certainty of evidence is low. Providers expressed higher satisfaction with the intervention (medication + laminaria) compared to the comparison (laminaria alone). The certainty of evidence is moderate. Fewer women in the intervention group (medication + laminaria) experienced side effects such as nausea, diarrhea, or bleeding compared to the comparison group (laminaria alone). The certainty of evidence for these outcomes ranges from low to high. Fewer women in the intervention group (medication + laminaria) required additional interventions compared to the comparison group (laminaria alone). The certainty of evidence is low. There was no difference in uterine perforation rates between the two groups. The certainty of evidence is low. Women in the intervention group (medication + laminaria) reported lower satisfaction rates compared to the comparison group (laminaria alone). The certainty of evidence is moderate. More women in the intervention group (medication + laminaria) experienced pre-procedure expulsion compared to the comparison group (laminaria alone). The certainty of evidence is moderate. More women in the intervention group (medication + laminaria) experienced post-procedure pain compared to the comparison group (laminaria alone). The certainty of evidence is high. For Sub-PICO 4, which compared two different mechanical methods (2 days of mechanical method versus 1 day of mechanical method), the following findings were observed: Pre-procedure cervical dilation was greater in the intervention group (2 days of mechanical method) compared to the comparison group (1 day of mechanical method). The certainty of evidence is moderate. The time to complete the procedure was shorter in the intervention group (2 days of mechanical method) compared to the comparison group (1 day of mechanical method). The certainty of evidence is low. More women in the intervention group (2 days of mechanical method) experienced post-procedure pain compared to the comparison group (1 day of mechanical method). The certainty of evidence is low. For the comparison between synthetic dilators and laminaria, the following findings were observed: Women in the intervention group (synthetic dilator) reported higher satisfaction rates compared to the comparison group (laminaria). The certainty of evidence is moderate. Fewer women in the intervention group (synthetic dilator) experienced side effects such as nausea or vomiting compared to the comparison group (laminaria). The certainty of evidence for these outcomes is high. There was no difference in the occurrence of diarrhea as a side effect between the two groups. The certainty of evidence is low. Fewer women in the intervention group (synthetic dilator) experienced post-procedure pain compared to the comparison group (laminaria). The certainty of evidence is high. Pre-procedure cervical dilation was lesser in the intervention group (synthetic dilator) compared to the comparison group (laminaria). The certainty of evidence is high. More women in the intervention group (synthetic dilator) required further dilation compared to the comparison group (laminaria). The certainty of evidence is high. The time to complete the procedure was shorter in the intervention group (synthetic dilator) compared to the comparison group (laminaria). The certainty of evidence is moderate. Additional criteria such as values, resource requirements, cost-effectiveness, equity, acceptability, and feasibility were also considered. However, there is significant uncertainty or variability in these aspects, and further research is needed to draw definitive conclusions.
